summary: In prison, Paul weighs life against death, finds Christ in both, and asks Philippi to live as citizens worthy of the gospel.

context.title: Life, death and citizenship
paragraphs: Paul writes to Philippi as a prisoner: his chains, he says, have become known throughout the praetorium. [c1] The nineteenth-century preacher Alexander MacLaren takes Rome as the place of writing. [c2] In verse 20 Paul hopes Christ will be magnified in his body, through life or through death, and the reading weighs those two outcomes. [c3]

Philippi was rebuilt by Philip II of Macedon and under Augustus became a Roman colony, as Acts 16:12 notes. [c4] Colonists sent from Rome stayed enrolled in its tribes, making the town a small Rome abroad. [c5] Paul’s verb in verse 27, about living as citizens, would strike such readers, and the letter later places their citizenship in heaven. [c6]

translationNotes.summary: Greek has no verb here: “to me the living, Christ”. Living is so full of Christ that his name sums it up.
translationNotes.body: The Greek puts “to me” first for emphasis and uses no verb. [c7] Bengel notes that the article marks “to live” as the subject, so Christ is the predicate. [c8] Calvin instead read Christ as gain to Paul in life and in death, a rendering the Pulpit Commentary judges weaker. [c9] Moule explains that living, for Paul, is so full of Christ that his name sums it up. [c10]

translationNotes.summary: Kerdos is plain gain or profit, the word Paul uses in 3:7 for advantages he later wrote off for Christ.
translationNotes.body: Kerdos means gain or advantage, a word in Greek use since Homer. [c11] In 3:7 Paul uses its plural for the advantages he once counted as gains and now counts as loss because of Christ. [c12] Ellicott explains why dying is gain here: death is a new stage in union with Christ. [c13] Paul does not despise life, for in verse 24 he judges staying more necessary for their sake. [c14]

translationNotes.summary: Analyō means to loosen; used of a ship slipping its moorings or of striking a tent or camp, it comes to mean “depart”.
translationNotes.body: The verb’s root sense is loosing or undoing. [c15] By usage it can mean a ship unmooring or a camp striking its tents, and so to depart. [c16] Ellicott inclines to the camp picture: the body is a tent, and death the last striking of it. [c17] The related noun appears in 2 Timothy 4:6 for Paul’s own coming death. [c18] Paul pairs departing with being with Christ, which Ellicott takes to follow immediately on death. [c19]

translationNotes.summary: Politeuesthe, from politēs, citizen, means “live as citizens”: a pointed word for readers in a Roman colony.
translationNotes.body: The verb means to be a citizen, or to behave as one. [c20] Moule renders it “live your citizen-life” in a way worthy of the gospel. [c21] In the New Testament it occurs only here and in Acts 23:1, and its cognate noun appears in 3:20, where the believers’ citizenship is in heaven. [c22] In Hellenistic Greek it can also simply mean to conduct one’s life by some rule. [c23]

claims.text: Paul writes as a prisoner: in Phil 1:7 he speaks of his bonds and in Phil 1:13 says they have become known in the whole praetorium.
Alexander MacLaren takes Paul to be writing to Philippi from Rome.
In Phil 1:20 Paul hopes Christ will be magnified in his body, whether through life or through death, and verses 21-26 take up the alternative of life or death.
Ellicott notes that Philippi was rebuilt by the father of Alexander the Great; Acts 16:12 calls it a colony, and Lumby says a Roman colony had been founded there by Augustus.
Roman colonists were sent out from Rome and their names remained enrolled in the lists of the tribes of Rome, so a colony was a bit of Rome on foreign soil.
Ellicott finds the citizenship verb of Phil 1:27 natural in writing to a Roman colony proud of its citizenship, and Phil 3:20 places the believers’ πολίτευμα in heaven.
In Phil 1:21 the Greek puts ἐμοί (to me) first, where it is strongly emphatic, and the clause τὸ ζῆν Χριστός has no verb.
Bengel notes that the article in τὸ ζῆν denotes the subject of the clause.
Calvin rendered the verse as Christ being gain to Paul in life and in death, a rendering the Pulpit Commentary judges “not so well”.
Moule (Cambridge Bible) explains that living is for Paul so full of Christ that “Christ” sums it up.
κέρδος means gain or advantage and is attested in Greek from Homer down.
In Phil 3:7 Paul says that what were gains (κέρδη) to him he has counted loss because of Christ.
Ellicott explains that death is gain because it is a new stage in the progress of union with Christ.
In Phil 1:24 Paul judges remaining in the flesh more necessary for the Philippians’ sake.
The root meaning of ἀναλύω has to do with loosing or undoing.
By usage ἀναλύω can refer to the unmooring of a ship or the striking of a tent or camp, and means to depart, including to depart from life.
Ellicott inclines (“perhaps better”) to the metaphor of striking tents and breaking camp, with death as the last striking of the tent.
The related noun ἀνάλυσις appears in 2 Tim 4:6 for the time of Paul’s departure.
Phil 1:23 joins departing with being with Christ, which Ellicott holds Paul contemplates as the immediate consequence of death.
In the middle voice πολιτεύω means to be a citizen, or to behave as a citizen.
Moule renders Phil 1:27 literally as “live your citizen-life in a way worthy of” the gospel.
In the New Testament the verb occurs only in Phil 1:27 and Acts 23:1, and the cognate noun πολίτευμα occurs in Phil 3:20.
In Hellenistic writings the verb can mean to conduct oneself according to some law of life, without emphasis on citizenship.
